justice: The disproportionate allocation of space to motorized lanes versus pedestrian paths demonstrates low spatial equity for non-motorized road users.
Lack of visible tactile paving (blind tracks) along the roadside fails to provide fairness for visually impaired users.
The absence of continuous, clearly defined sidewalks and visible curb ramps on the right side severely limits accessibility for wheelchair users and older adults.
safety: Wide, straight multi-lane roads encourage high vehicle speeds, posing a significant risk to adolescents and older adults if crossing.
The non-motorized lane/shoulder is only separated by a painted solid white line, lacking physical barriers to protect cyclists from fast-moving vehicles.
Regularly spaced street lighting poles provide essential illumination, enhancing nighttime visibility and basic safety for all road users.
livability: The complete absence of ground-floor commercial units or community facilities fails to support the daily needs and social activities of all social groups.
A lack of resting facilities, such as benches or seating areas, prevents older adults from comfortably engaging in the outdoor environment.
No visible pedestrian activity or 'eyes on the street' reduces social surveillance, making the environment feel isolated and less inviting for teenagers and vulnerable groups.
sustainability: Dense rows of planted trees and hedges along both sides of the road act as carbon sinks and support urban greening.
The vast expanse of impermeable asphalt paving lacks visible rainwater infiltration facilities, negatively impacting sustainable stormwater management.
The absence of visible public transit infrastructure, such as bus stops, fails to encourage low-carbon mass transit travel for residents.
aesthetics: The road surface is highly clean and well-maintained, contributing to a tidy visual environment for drivers.
Continuous green hedges and dense trees provide a consistent and pleasant visual boundary to the streetscape.
Prominent overhead power lines and purely utilitarian street structures introduce visual clutter that slightly detracts from the sky view.
comfort: The lack of benches or stopping points results in extremely poor physical comfort for older adults who require periodic rest.
Trees are set far back behind curbs, providing insufficient direct canopy shade over the road edges, which reduces thermal comfort for cyclists in summer.
Close proximity to wide, high-speed motorized traffic lanes likely generates high noise levels, lowering psychological comfort for pedestrians and cyclists.
walkability: The lack of a dedicated, continuous sidewalk on the immediate right side forces pedestrians to share space with vehicles or walk on landscaping.
No pedestrian crosswalks or traffic calming measures are visible, creating severe barriers to safe route connectivity for all social groups.
The absence of street-level frontage activity and long uninterrupted blocks makes walking visually monotonous and physically exhausting for older adults.
bikeability: The wide, paved shoulder provides a flat surface for cycling, but lacks colored lane markings to clearly designate it as a dedicated bike lane.
The lack of physical separation (such as bollards or planters) exposes cyclists, including adolescents, to high-speed vehicular conflicts.
No bicycle parking facilities or rest nodes are present along the visible stretch, reducing the convenience of cycling as a practical transport mode.
